title: Discriminated unions
description: Learn how discriminated unions make complex React state and API responses type-safe and easy to maintain.

data.text: A discriminated union is a set of object types that share one common property with a literal type. That shared property, called the discriminant, tells TypeScript exactly which shape you are working with. It is one of the most useful patterns for modeling state in React.

React components often have several loading states: idle, loading, success, and error. Each state carries different data. A discriminated union lets you express all of these states in one type and safely access the right fields.

data.title: Async State as a Discriminated Union
data.content: Modeling fetch states with a common kind field

data.text: Without a discriminant, TypeScript cannot tell which properties are available in a union. The `kind` property acts as a key that unlocks the rest of the object. In the example above, TypeScript knows that `state.data` only exists when `state.kind` is `'success'`, so accessing `state.data` in any other case would be a compile-time error.

data.title: Union Types with and without Discrimination

cards.title: Without a Discriminant
cards.description: TypeScript must check every property before it knows which fields exist. The code becomes harder to write and easier to misuse.

cards.title: With a Discriminant
cards.description: A single literal field tells TypeScript exactly which shape is active. The compiler narrows automatically in switch statements and if checks.
cons: Requires a consistent property across all variants

data.text: Discriminated unions appear everywhere in React: form submission states, route guards, modal dialogs, and even event handlers. Grouping related states under one type makes components predictable and self-documenting.

data.title: Form Submission State
data.content: Using a discriminated union for form status

data.title: Choose a Clear Discriminant Name
data.text: Common names include `kind`, `type`, `status`, and `variant`. Pick a name that describes what changes across variants, and keep it consistent across your codebase so other developers know what to expect.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A discriminated union shares one literal property across all variants
TypeScript narrows automatically when you check that property
Use them for async states, forms, modals, and route guards
Combine with exhaustive checking for compile-time safety
data.takeaway: Discriminated unions turn messy conditional logic into predictable, type-safe state machines.
